# Sample time stamps

RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens used by unit tests. They are not issued by a real time stamping authority. The ECDSA tokens below are signed with the `es256` test key and certificate in `../raw_signature`, and stamp the binary string "some sample content to sign".

* `unsorted_signed_attrs.tst` - the signed attributes are encoded in the order `messageDigest`, `contentType`, which is not the sorted order DER requires, and the signature covers that encoding.
* `signing_time_after_expiry.tst` - `genTime` is 2025-01-01, within the certificate's validity. The CMS `signingTime` signed attribute is 2031-01-01, after the certificate expires.

RFC 5652 sections 5.3 and 5.4 require DER-encoded signed attributes, including canonical `SET OF` ordering. The unsorted fixture is deliberately nonconforming and tests an interoperability allowance; accepting it does not make its encoding RFC-compliant.

The unit tests also construct forged tokens by changing the `TSTInfo` message imprint and a second signer's `messageDigest` while copying the genuine signature. They assert rejection for both signer orders, for a modified signer alone, and for duplicate signatures in both unsorted and correctly DER-sorted tokens. A single correctly DER-sorted signer remains valid.

## RSA signature profiles

`ps256.tst`, `ps384.tst`, `ps512.tst`, `ps256-salt0.tst`,
`ps256-saltmax.tst`, and `rsa-pkcs1.tst` are synthetic offline CMS
timestamp tokens generated by `python3 generate_rsa.py` with OpenSSL 3.
They embed the same RSA-2048 TSA certificate with `rsaEncryption` SPKI and
sign a TSTInfo whose SHA-256 message imprint covers
`b"RSA timestamp regression"`. The attested time lies within the embedded
certificate's validity. Tests do not depend on the current time or a network TSA.

The PS256/384/512 tokens use MGF1 with the signature hash and a hash-length
salt. The salt-zero and maximum-salt tokens have cryptographically valid
signatures but do not satisfy the supported PS profiles. The PKCS#1 v1.5
token preserves legacy TSA interoperability. Tests mutate unsigned CMS
algorithm parameters to check declared versus actual parameters, and mutate
the embedded certificate's SPKI to exercise PSS key restrictions without
changing the RSA key. Those mutated certificates are not trust fixtures.

The generator verifies every token with OpenSSL CMS before saving it. It
generates a new synthetic key and certificate on each run; the private key
is temporary and is never saved in the repository.
